paragraphs.simple: Alice was not surprised that the Rabbit talked to himself and said that he would be late. Later she thought about it and saw that she should have been surprised, but at the time it seemed normal. Then the Rabbit took a watch out of his waistcoat pocket, looked at it, and hurried away. Alice jumped up. She had never seen a rabbit with a pocket in its coat or a watch to take out of it. She wanted so much to know more that she ran across the field after him. She was just in time to see him go down a big hole under the hedge.

paragraphs.context: she knelt down and looked along the passage into the loveliest garden
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice finds a tiny door that opens to a beautiful garden, but she is too big to go through. She wishes she could shut up like a telescope.
paragraphs.simple: Alice opened the door and found a small way through that was not much bigger than a hole for a rat. She went down on her knees and looked through it into the most beautiful garden she had ever seen. She wanted so much to leave the dark hall and walk among the bright flowers and cool fountains. But she could not even push her head through the door. She thought that even if her head went through, it would not be much use without her shoulders. She wished she could become small like a telescope that is pushed shorter. She thought she could do it if she only knew how to start. So many strange things had happened lately that she began to think almost nothing was truly impossible.

paragraphs.context: I’m sure I’m not Ada
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice is not sure who she is. She tests herself with numbers and a poem, but she gets them wrong, so she thinks she has changed into another girl.
paragraphs.simple: Alice said that she was sure she was not Ada, because Ada has long curls and hers are not curly. She was sure she was not Mabel either, because she herself knows many things and Mabel knows very little. She felt confused. She tried to remember what she knew. She said numbers and the capitals of countries, and she got everything wrong. She thought she must have changed into Mabel. She folded her hands on her lap, like a child saying a lesson, and tried to say a poem. But her voice sounded rough and strange, and the words were not the same as before.

paragraphs.context: There is such a nice little dog near our house
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice talks happily about her neighbour's dog, but she forgets that mice are afraid of dogs. The Mouse swims away.
paragraphs.simple: Alice quickly wanted to talk about something else. She asked the Mouse if it liked dogs. The Mouse did not answer, so she went on in an excited voice. She said there was a nice little dog near her house. It had bright eyes and long curly brown hair. It would bring back things that you threw, and sit up and ask for its dinner. It belonged to a farmer, who said it was worth a hundred pounds because it killed all the rats. Alice then saw that she had upset the Mouse again. The Mouse was swimming away as fast as it could and was making a lot of noise in the water.

paragraphs.context: are you all ready? This is the driest thing I know
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Mouse says he will make everyone dry by reading a dull history lesson. It is a joke, because the lesson does not dry anyone.
paragraphs.simple: The Mouse spoke with a serious look. He asked if everyone was ready and said that this was the driest thing he knew. He asked for silence. Then he read from a history book. It said that William the Conqueror was helped by the pope and that the English soon obeyed him, because they wanted leaders and were used to new rulers who took power by force. The leaders of two parts of England were mentioned.

paragraphs.context: they began running when they liked, and left off when they liked
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Dodo organises a strange race with no start and no end. In the end everyone has won.
paragraphs.simple: First the Dodo marked a path for the race in the shape of a circle, and said the exact shape did not matter. Then all the animals stood in different places along the path. Nobody said "go". They began to run when they wanted, and stopped when they wanted, so it was hard to know when the race had ended. After about half an hour, when they were all dry again, the Dodo suddenly shouted that the race was over. They all crowded around him, breathing fast, and asked who had won.

paragraphs.context: Where’s the other ladder
paragraphs.mainIdea: The animals outside are trying to get the Rabbit's house in order, and they are making a lot of noise. Bill is told to go down the chimney.
paragraphs.simple: Alice waited for some time and heard nothing. Then she heard small wheels and many voices at the same time. The voices asked where the other ladder was, and said that only one was brought, because Bill had the other. They told Bill to bring it. They said to put the ladders at the corner, to tie them together because they were not long enough, and not to worry too much. Then someone shouted a warning about a rope and a loose slate on the roof, and something fell with a loud crash. They asked who did it and thought it was Bill. Then they argued about who should go down the chimney. In the end they said the master wanted Bill to go.

paragraphs.context: the puppy jumped into the air off all its feet at once
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice plays with a giant puppy. She is more afraid of being stepped on than of being bitten.
paragraphs.simple: Almost without thinking, Alice picked up a little stick and held it out to the puppy. The puppy jumped into the air with all four feet off the ground and made a happy cry. It ran to the stick and pretended to bite it. Alice jumped behind a big thistle so that the puppy would not run over her. When she came out, the puppy ran at the stick again and fell over in its hurry. Alice thought it was like playing with a big cart horse and was afraid it would step on her, so she ran round the plant again. The puppy made many short runs at the stick, a little way forward and a long way back, and barked in a rough voice. At last it sat down far away, breathing fast, with its tongue out and its large eyes nearly closed.

paragraphs.context: So she began nibbling at the righthand bit again
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice gets back to her right size. She is careful when she sees a small house, and makes herself even smaller so that she does not frighten the people inside.
paragraphs.simple: It had been so long since she was the right size that it felt strange at first. After a few minutes she was used to it and began to talk to herself. She said that half of her plan was done and that all the changes were very confusing. Now she had her right size, so the next step was to get to the beautiful garden. Then she suddenly saw a small house, about four feet high. She thought she should not come to it at this size because she would scare the people living there. So she ate more of the right-hand piece of mushroom, and did not go near the house until she was about nine inches high.

paragraphs.context: a footman in livery came running out of the wood
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice watches two footmen, one with a fish-like face and one with a frog-like face. They are delivering an invitation to the Duchess.
paragraphs.simple: After a minute or two, Alice stood and looked at the house and did not know what to do. Suddenly a man servant in special clothes came running out of the wood. She knew he was a servant because of his clothes. If she had looked only at his face, she would have said he was a fish. He knocked loudly on the door with his hands. Another servant opened it. He had a round face and big eyes, like a frog. Alice saw that both men had powdered hair that was curly all over. She wanted to know what was happening, so she moved a little out of the wood to listen.

paragraphs.context: As soon as she had made out the proper way of nursing it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice takes the baby outside. The baby turns into a pig.
paragraphs.simple: When Alice understood how to hold the baby (by twisting it into a kind of knot and holding its right ear and left foot so that it could not come undone), she took it out into the open air. She thought that if she left the child there, they would surely kill it in a day or two, and that would be wrong. She said this aloud. The little thing made a short sound like a pig. She told it that it was not a good way to speak.

paragraphs.context: if you only kept on good terms with him
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Hatter says that Time is a person. He says that if you are friends with Time, he will make the clock go at any speed you like.
paragraphs.simple: The Hatter said that if Alice knew Time as well as he did, she would not speak of wasting it, because Time is a person. He said that Time does not like to be hit. He said that if you were friendly with Time, he would do almost anything with the clock. For example, if it were nine in the morning and time to start lessons, you could just whisper a word to Time, and the clock would go round at once to half past one, time for dinner.

paragraphs.context: she found herself at last in the beautiful garden
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice remembers what she has learned. She uses the key and the mushroom to get small and finally enters the garden.
paragraphs.simple: Once more she was in the long hall near the small glass table. She said that she would do better this time. She took the little golden key and opened the door to the garden. Then she ate pieces of the mushroom, which she had kept in her pocket, until she was about one foot tall. After that she walked down the little passage. At last she was in the beautiful garden with the bright flower beds and the cool fountains.

paragraphs.context: this here ought to have been a red rose-tree
paragraphs.mainIdea: Three card gardeners explain that they planted a white rose tree by mistake. They are painting the roses red so that the Queen does not find out.
paragraphs.simple: Five and Seven said nothing but looked at Two. Two began to talk in a low voice. He called Alice "Miss" and said that this tree should have been a red rose tree, but they had planted a white one by mistake. If the Queen found out, they would all have their heads cut off. So they were doing their best to fix it before she came. Then Five, who was looking across the garden with fear, shouted that the Queen was coming, and the three gardeners at once threw themselves flat on their faces. Alice heard many footsteps and looked round, hoping to see the Queen.

paragraphs.context: The chief difficulty Alice found at first was in managing her flamingo
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice finds croquet very hard because the mallet is a flamingo, the balls are hedgehogs, and the soldiers who make the arches move away.
paragraphs.simple: Alice found it very hard to control her flamingo at first. She could easily put its body under her arm with its legs hanging down. But just when she had its neck straight and was ready to hit the hedgehog with its head, the bird would twist round and look up at her with such a puzzled face that she could not stop laughing. And when she had its head down and was ready to start again, it was annoying to see that the hedgehog had opened up and was crawling away. There was also often a raised line or a low place in the ground in the way, and the soldiers who made the arches kept standing up and walking to other parts of the field. Soon Alice decided that this was a very hard game.

paragraphs.context: When I’m a Duchess
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice dreams of being a Duchess. She thinks pepper makes people angry and other things make people sour or sweet.
paragraphs.simple: Alice said to herself, without much hope, that when she was a Duchess she would have no pepper in her kitchen. She said soup was fine without it. Maybe pepper was what made people angry, vinegar was what made them sour, and chamomile was what made them bitter. And sweets made children kind. She was happy about her new idea. She wished people knew it, because then they would not be so unwilling to give such things to children.

paragraphs.context: I dare say you’re wondering why I don’t put my arm round your waist
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Duchess says she is afraid of Alice's flamingo. They talk, and the Duchess ends each thing with a "moral".
paragraphs.simple: The Duchess said after a short stop that she supposed Alice was wondering why she did not put her arm round Alice's waist. She said the reason was that she did not trust the flamingo's temper and asked if she should try the experiment.

paragraphs.context: Will you walk a little faster
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Mock Turtle sings a song in which a whiting asks a snail to join a dance in the sea. The snail says it is too far.
paragraphs.simple: A whiting asked a snail to walk a little faster, because a porpoise was close and stepping on his tail. He said the lobsters and turtles were all coming eagerly to the stones on the beach and asked the snail to join the dance. The whiting said the snail could not know how nice it would be when they were thrown with the lobsters into the sea. But the snail said that it was too far and looked away with doubt. He thanked the whiting nicely but said he would not dance. The whiting's friend asked what it mattered how far they went, as there was another shore on the other side, nearer to France. He asked the snail not to be afraid but to come and dance.

paragraphs.context: The King and Queen of Hearts were seated on their throne
paragraphs.mainIdea: The trial begins. The Knave of Hearts is a prisoner, and the court is full of animals and playing cards.
paragraphs.simple: The King and Queen of Hearts were sitting on their throne when Alice came. A large crowd had gathered around them, with all kinds of small birds and animals and a whole set of cards. The Knave stood in front of them with chains on him, and a soldier on each side. The White Rabbit stood near the King with a trumpet in one hand and a roll of old paper in the other. In the middle of the room was a table with a large dish of tarts. They looked so good that Alice felt hungry. She wished they would finish the trial and give out the food. But it seemed that this would not happen, so she looked at everything around her to pass the time.

paragraphs.context: The trial cannot proceed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice upsets the jury box by accident. She puts the jurors back, but one has the wrong end of the body up and cannot move. The King stops the trial until all the jurors are in place.
paragraphs.simple: The King said in a very serious voice that the trial could not go on until all the jurymen were back in their right places. He said the word "all" with strong emphasis and looked hard at Alice.

paragraphs.context: So she sat on, with closed eyes, and half believed herself in Wonderland
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice wakes up from her dream, but with her eyes closed she imagines that everything in Wonderland is just sounds from the real world.
paragraphs.simple: So she stayed sitting with her eyes shut, and half believed she was still in Wonderland, though she knew that if she opened them, all would turn into boring real life. She knew that the grass would be just moving in the wind and the pool would be moving in small waves with the plants. The noise of cups would turn into the sound of bells on sheep. The Queen's loud cries would become the voice of a boy who looks after sheep. The baby's sneeze, the Gryphon's cry, and all the other strange sounds would turn into the mixed noise of a busy farm. And the sound of the cows far away would take the place of the Mock Turtle's heavy sobs.

sentences.context: it occurred to her that she ought to have wondered at this
sentences.simple: It came into her mind that she should have been surprised by this.
sentences.grammar: "Ought to have" + a past participle talks about something that was right to do but that did not happen. "It occurred to her" means "she suddenly thought of it".

sentences.context: and even if my head would go through
sentences.simple: And even if my head could go through the door,
sentences.grammar: "Even if ... would" talks about something that is not true now and may never be true. The sentence goes on to say what would still be a problem.

sentences.context: I must have been changed for Mabel
sentences.simple: I think I have been turned into Mabel.
sentences.grammar: "Must have" + a past participle shows that the speaker is almost sure that something happened in the past. Here Alice tries to explain her strange feelings.

sentences.context: I wish I hadn’t cried so much
sentences.simple: I am sorry that I cried so much.
sentences.grammar: "I wish I had not" + a past participle shows that you are sorry about something that you did in the past and cannot change.

sentences.context: not that she wanted much to know
sentences.simple: It was not because she really wanted to know.
sentences.grammar: "Not that" adds a short comment that corrects what you just said. It means "I do not say that...". Here Alice asks a question out of politeness, not because she is very interested.

sentences.context: as it can’t possibly make me larger, it must make me smaller
sentences.simple: Because it cannot make me bigger, it has to make me smaller.
sentences.grammar: The sentence uses two clauses to give a reason: "as" means "because". "Must" shows that Alice is sure about her conclusion, though her thinking is funny.

sentences.context: I can’t remember things as I used
sentences.simple: I cannot remember things the way I could before.
sentences.grammar: "As I used" is a short form of "as I used to (remember them)". The words "to remember" are left out because the meaning is clear.

sentences.context: she would have called him a fish
sentences.simple: She would have said that he was a fish.
sentences.grammar: This is "would have" + a past participle. It tells what Alice would have done if she had looked only at his face. The condition is in the part "judging by his face only".

sentences.simple: If the baby had become an adult,
sentences.grammar: "If it had grown up" and "it would have made" talk about something that did not happen. This kind of sentence is used for a past situation that cannot change.

sentences.context: If you knew Time as well as I do
sentences.simple: If you knew Time as well as I do,
sentences.grammar: This is a second conditional sentence: "If you knew ..., you wouldn't ...". It talks about a situation that is not true now. The Hatter says Alice does not know Time well.

sentences.simple: It would be wise for you not to talk.
sentences.grammar: "Had better" + a base verb gives strong advice or a warning. "You'd better not" is a short form of "you had better not". It can sound like a threat.

sentences.context: I should have croqueted the Queen’s hedgehog just now
sentences.simple: I would have hit the Queen's hedgehog just now with my ball,
sentences.grammar: "Should have" + a past participle talks about something that would have happened but did not. The verb "croqueted" is a made-up verb from the noun "croquet", used by Alice.

sentences.context: I think I should understand that better
sentences.simple: I think I would understand that better if someone wrote it down for me.
sentences.grammar: "If I had it written down" uses "have + object + past participle". It means that someone else does the writing, so that Alice has it in written form.

sentences.context: so you can have no idea what a delightful thing a Lobster Quadrille is
sentences.simple: So you cannot imagine how nice a Lobster Quadrille is.
sentences.grammar: "What a delightful thing ... is" is an exclamation inside a longer sentence. "Can have no idea" means "cannot imagine".

sentences.context: she thought, and rightly too, that very few little girls of her age knew the meaning of it at all
sentences.simple: She thought, and she was right, that very few girls of her age knew what it meant.
sentences.grammar: The words "and rightly too" are an extra comment between commas. The main idea is that Alice was proud to know the word "jurors".

sentences.context: though she knew she had but to open them again
sentences.simple: though she knew that she only had to open her eyes again
sentences.grammar: "Had but to" is an old-fashioned way to say "only had to". Here it shows how easy it is for Alice to leave her dream.

account for.meaning: To explain why something happens. "That accounts for it" means "That explains it". "No accounting for tastes" means you cannot explain why people like different things.
account for.example: “Ah! that accounts for it,” said the Hatter.

after all.meaning: In spite of what was said or planned before.
after all.example: after all it might tell her something worth hearing

at any rate.example: at any rate it would not open any of them

by the way.meaning: Used to add something that is not the main point.

come to an end.example: Would the fall never come to an end

doze off.meaning: To fall into a light sleep.

get hold of.meaning: To take something in the hand; to catch it.

give oneself airs.meaning: To act as if you are better than other people.

hold one's tongue.meaning: To stop talking; to be quiet. It is not polite.

in a hurry.example: in a great hurry to change the subject

make out.meaning: To see, hear or understand something with difficulty.

make up one's mind.example: made up my mind about it

no use.meaning: Not helpful; without any good result.
no use.example: there’s no use in crying like that

out of one's wits.meaning: "Frighten out of one's wits" means to frighten very much.
out of one's wits.example: frighten them out of their wits

put on.meaning: To place clothes on your body.
put on.example: she had put on one of the Rabbit’s little white kid gloves

race course.meaning: A track or piece of ground where races are run. Here the Dodo draws a rough circle on the ground for the Caucus-race.
race course.example: First it marked out a race-course, in a sort of circle

take a fancy to.meaning: To start to like someone or something.

take up.meaning: To lift something and pick it up.

think nothing of.meaning: To feel that something is easy or not important.
think nothing of.example: I shall think nothing of tumbling down stairs

tired of.meaning: Not wanting any more of something, because you have had too much.
tired of.example: very tired of sitting by her sister

to begin with.meaning: At first; as the first thing.

turn out.meaning: To make someone leave a place.
turn out.example: be turned out of the house
